## The idea

The pieces in this book leave behind repeated code: event playback, bar
validation, transposition, chord voicing, articulation, and source reporting.
Extract a helper after you have written it more than twice and can name its
stable inputs. Earlier extraction risks preserving guesses as an API.
Begin this refactor after completing at least one of Lessons 55-57. A capstone
provides real call sites, edge cases, and provenance fields; without them, the
library design is still speculation.

Settle on one event schema. The common keys are :note, :start, and :duration,
with :amp when dynamics belong to score data. Migrate older pieces instead of
teaching the library several aliases for duration.

Keep the framework small enough that the score remains visible. A helper should
remove accidental machinery, not hide musical decisions. Write a README for
the version of you who returns in six months and no longer remembers why
events use absolute starts or where articulation is applied.

## Run this

This fresh buffer contains a compact library surface and one score. Validation,
transposition, and rendering share the same event schema.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 78

define :validate_events do |events, expected_end|
  raise "empty score" if events.empty?

  events.each do |event|
    required = [:note, :start, :duration]
    missing = required.reject { |key| event.key?(key) }
    raise "missing keys: #{missing}" unless missing.empty?
    raise "duration must be positive" unless event[:duration] > 0
  end

  actual_end = events.map { |event| event[:start] + event[:duration] }.max
  raise "expected end #{expected_end}, got #{actual_end}" unless actual_end == expected_end
end

define :transpose_events do |events, semitones|
  events.map do |event|
    event.merge(note: note(event[:note]) + semitones)
  end
end

define :play_events do |events, synth_name|
  use_synth synth_name
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note],
      release: event[:duration] * 0.82,
      amp: event.fetch(:amp, 0.8)
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep events.last[:duration]
end

theme = [
  {note: :c4, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.65},
  {note: :e4, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.72},
  {note: :g4, start: 2.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.8},
  {note: :c5, start: 3.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.9}
]

validate_events theme, 4.0
play_events theme, :piano
sleep 1
play_events transpose_events(theme, 7), :pluck
```

The second phrase moves up a fifth. The original hashes remain unchanged
because transpose_events returns a new array.

## Change one thing

1. Remove duration from one event. Validation reports the schema error before
   playback. Restore it, then add an unknown key and observe that the helper
   ignores extension data it does not need.
2. Change transpose_events to mutate event[:note] in place. The first array now
   changes after transposition, which makes later comparisons unreliable.
   Restore the merge-based version.
3. Add an articulation key and a narrow release helper that maps :legato,
   :detached, and :accent to renderer options. Keep pitch, start, and duration
   handling outside that helper.

## Why it works

A small library gives repeated representations one authority. When every piece
uses :duration, a validation fix applies everywhere. When transposition always
returns new events, callers know whether their source data is preserved.
Predictable contracts are more useful than a large catalogue of wrappers.

The helper names expose levels of abstraction. play_events handles the general
timeline. play_phrase is appropriate for a sequential array where each event
starts after the previous duration. A chord renderer can remain local until
several pieces need the same voicing policy.

README documentation should explain choices rather than restate names. Record
why starts are absolute, whether amp belongs to score or performance data, how
rests are represented, whether tied notes become one event, and which Sonic Pi
version the examples target. Include one minimal fresh-buffer example and the
manual audition steps.

Version the library beside the pieces that use it. A schema migration should
be visible in both helper code and score data. Avoid compatibility branches
that allow :duration, :dur, and :length forever; they move complexity into
every future function.

The final capability is practical: take a printed score or a short recording,
turn it into editable code, and explain the theory represented by the data.
The library supports that work. It is not the work itself.

## Take it further

Collect helpers used by at least three finished pieces. Produce one small
library file, one README, and a migration of two older scores to the settled
schema. Required helpers are event validation, play_events, transposition, and
one articulation or voicing function. The constraint is that each migrated
score remains readable without opening the helper definitions. Record Ruby
syntax results and leave Sonic Pi auditioning as manual QA.
